claims.source: We found that KCNQ2-R581Q alone or combined with wildtype KCNQ2 produced 81.6% (t test: p<0.0001) and 56.6% (t test: p=0.006) smaller current density, respectively, as compared to cells expressing wild-type channels (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The findings are consistent with a KCNQ2 loss-of-function.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with a KCNQ2 loss-of-function.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: iPSCs were derived from PBMCs using integration-free, Sendai virus-mediated reprogramming.
claims.source: We derived iPSCs from PBMCs using integration-free, Sendai virus-mediated reprogramming.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claims.claim: An isogenic mutation-corrected control iPSC line was generated from the patient-derived line using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
claims.source: To create a model that would allow us to attribute any phenotypic differences to the disease-associated genetic variant, we generated an isogenic mutation-corrected control iPSC line from the patient-derived line (Figure 1C). We specifically corrected the mutant allele using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and simultaneously introduced two silent mutations in the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) to prevent re-cleavage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study, supported by Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The resulting iPSCs exhibited a normal female karyotype, typical stem cell morphology, and expressed pluripotency markers, including nuclear NANOG and the cell surface antigen SSEA4.
claims.source: The resulting iPSCs exhibited a normal female karyotype, typical stem cell morphology, and expressed pluripotency markers, including nuclear NANOG and the cell surface antigen SSEA4 (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: No evidence for off-target edits was found in any of the top 10 predicted genomic regions with homology to the targeted KCNQ2 exon using a T7 endonuclease-based assay.
claims.source: We found no evidence for off-target edits in any of the top 10 predicted genomic regions with homology to the targeted KCNQ2 exon using a T7 endonuclease-based assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Whole genome sequencing confirmed the genetic correction and integrity of the targeted gene, and found that there were no edits in any of all 74 predicted off-target sites.
claims.source: As an additional quality control, we performed whole genome sequencing (WGS) of samples Q2-04R581Q/+ (29.41x coverage) and isoQ2-04+/+ (28.12x coverage) and determined that they correspond to the same individual (pi_hat score = 0.99). We also validated the genetic correction and integrity of the targeted gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and found that there were no edits in any of all 74 predicted off-target sites indicating highly specific CRISPR activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, inner arrows, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and 3B.

claims.claim: Cortical excitatory neurons were differentiated through a modified NGN2 overexpression protocol.
claims.source: Given the clinical presentation of KCNQ2-associated DEE and the focal source of seizures that reside in the cortex (Wilmshurst et al., 2015; Fisher et al., 2017), we chose to study cortical excitatory neurons, differentiated through a modified NGN2 overexpression protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A; Zhang et al., 2013; Nehme et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Over 95% of GFP-positive cells were also MAP2-positive for all iPSC lines.
claims.source: Over 95% of GFP-positive cells were also MAP2-positive for all iPSC lines.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: All neurons that were GFP and MAP2 positive also expressed vGLUT1.
claims.source: Furthermore, all neurons that were GFP and MAP2 positive also expressed vGLUT1 (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claims.claim: The differentiated neuronal cultures expressed high levels of vGLUT2, FOXG1, and BRN2, which are characteristic of excitatory layer 2/3 cortical neurons.
claims.source: As previously described (Zhang et al., 2013), we found that these cultures expressed high levels of vGLUT2, FOXG1, and BRN2, which are characteristic of excitatory layer 2/3 cortical neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D and Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D and citations.

claims.claim: The differentiated neuronal cultures expressed several KCNQ2 splice variants by RT-qPCR.
claims.source: Importantly, we confirmed that the differentiated neuronal cultures expressed several KCNQ2 splice variants by RT-qPCR (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: One of the clinical hallmarks of KCNQ2-DEE is an interictal burst-suppression pattern recorded by EEG during the first few days of life.
claims.source: One of the clinical hallmarks of KCNQ2-DEE is an interictal burst-suppression pattern (i.e. paroxysmal bursts of activity interspersed with periods of electrical silence) recorded by EEG during the first few days of life (Weckhuysen et al., 2012; Milh et al., 2013; Millichap et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited a significantly greater number of active electrodes and slightly higher spontaneous firing frequency early in their maturation (DIV: 10-13), relative to isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited a significantly greater number of active electrodes (p<0.0001) and slightly higher spontaneous firing frequency (p=0.0081) early in their maturation (DIV: 10-13), relative to isoQ2-04+/+ neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons can fire spontaneously earlier than isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: This suggests that Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons are able to fire spontaneously earlier than isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The number of active electrodes was not different between Q2-04R581Q/+ and isoQ2-04+/+ neurons at later times in culture (DIV: 15-31).
claims.source: However, the number of active electrodes was not different between Q2-04R581Q/+ and isoQ2-04+/+ neurons at later times in culture (DIV: 15-31) (p=0.0896; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The distribution of spiking in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons was dramatically and increasingly irregular compared to isogenic control neurons, indicated by the increased inter-spike interval coefficient of variation (ISI CoV).
claims.source: More strikingly, the distribution of spiking in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons was dramatically and increasingly irregular compared to isogenic control neurons, indicated by the increased inter-spike interval coefficient of variation (ISI CoV; p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The irregularity in spiking was associated with greater bursting propensity, with short intervals between spikes in bursts and longer intervals between bursts.
claims.source: This irregularity was associated with greater bursting propensity, with short intervals between spikes in bursts and longer intervals between bursts.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Compared to isogenic control neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had increased average number of bursts detected on single electrodes.
claims.source: Compared to isogenic control neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had increased average number of bursts detected on single electrodes (repeated measures ANOVA for genotype: F(1,455) = 17.31, ***p<0.0001; genotype/day interaction: F(7,455) = 3.88, ###p=0.0004)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Compared to isogenic control neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had increased number of spikes within bursts.
claims.source: number of spikes within bursts (repeated measures ANOVA for genotype: F(1,455) = 17.31, ***p<0.0001; genotype/day interaction: F(7,455) = 2.24, #p=0.0301)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Compared to isogenic control neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had increased percentage of all detected spikes which were found to occur within bursts.
claims.source: and percentage of all detected spikes which were found to occur within bursts (repeated measures ANOVA for genotype: F(1,455) = 135.47, ***p<0.0001; genotype/day interaction: F(7,455) = 5.89, ###p<0.0001; See Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons were more prone to fire in bursts rather than single tonic spikes compared to isogenic control neurons.
claims.source: These results indicate that Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons were more prone to fire in bursts rather than single tonic spikes compared to isogenic control neurons (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The bursting phenotype became even more pronounced and phasic over time.
claims.source: Moreover, the significant interaction of genotype and day in culture suggest that this bursting phenotype became even more pronounced and phasic over time.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons developed significantly smaller inter-burst interval CoV only after day 22 in culture, and thus their bursts became more regular and phasic.
claims.source: This is further supported by the fact that Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons developed significantly smaller inter-burst interval CoV only after day 22 in culture, and thus their bursts became more regular and phasic (p=0.0169; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had a significantly more depolarized RMP and higher input resistance only during week 3.
claims.source: However, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had a significantly more depolarized RMP (p=0.0163) and higher input resistance (p=0.0075) only during week 3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Table 1.

claims.claim: The increasing AP amplitudes for both genotypes over the course of 5 weeks indicate some progress in functional neuronal maturation.
claims.source: The increasing AP amplitudes for both genotypes over the course of 5 weeks indicate some progress in functional neuronal maturation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Table 1; Bardy et al., 2016; Nehme et al., 2018; Lindhout et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations.

claims.claim: Compared with isoQ2-04+/+ neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had slower AP repolarization with longer AP half-width at week 3.
claims.source: We observed that compared with isoQ2-04+/+ neurons, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had slower AP repolarization with longer AP half-width at week 3 (p=0.0383; Figure 3C,D; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and Table 1.

claims.claim: Slower AP repolarization is consistent with a reduced M-current.
claims.source: Slower AP repolarization is consistent with a reduced M-current.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on known properties of M-current.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons progressively developed faster AP repolarization with shorter AP half-widths at week 5.
claims.source: However, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons progressively developed faster AP repolarization with shorter AP half-widths at week 5 and larger fast component of the AHP (fAHP) at week 4 (p=0.03) and at week 5 (p=0.035; Figure 3C,D and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and Table 1.

claims.claim: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons had larger fast component of the AHP (fAHP) at week 4 and at week 5.
claims.source: However, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons progressively developed faster AP repolarization with shorter AP half-widths at week 5 and larger fast component of the AHP (fAHP) at week 4 (p=0.03) and at week 5 (p=0.035; Figure 3C,D and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D and Table 1.

claims.claim: There was no difference in AP thresholds between Q2-04R581Q/+ and isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: There was no difference in AP thresholds.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Faster AP repolarization would enable neurons to fire a greater number of APs more rapidly with less synaptic input, which may explain the enhanced number of spikes per burst and higher tendency of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons to fire within bursts.
claims.source: Faster AP repolarization would enable neurons to fire a greater number of APs more rapidly with less synaptic input, which may explain the enhanced number of spikes per burst and higher tendency of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons to fire within bursts (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Previous studies have shown the involvement of KCNQ2 channels in the medium AHP (mAHP) in cortical neurons.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown the involvement of KCNQ2 channels in the medium AHP (mAHP) in cortical neurons (Guan et al., 2011; Battefeld et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Compared to controls, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited significantly larger mAHPs (peak of AHP) and slow post-burst AHPs (sAHP; 1 s after last stimulus).
claims.source: Compared to controls, Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited significantly larger mAHPs (peak of AHP) and slow post-burst AHPs (sAHP; 1 s after last stimulus; p<0.0001 and p<0.0001, respectively; Figure 3E,F and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, F and Table 1.

claims.claim: Isogenic control neurons exhibited a time-dependent attenuation in the mAHP and sAHP and thus were significantly smaller than Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons during weeks 4–5 but not earlier.
claims.source: Surprisingly, isogenic control neurons exhibited a time-dependent attenuation in the mAHP and sAHP and thus were significantly smaller than Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons during weeks 4–5 but not earlier (Figure 3E,F and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, F and Table 1.

claims.claim: An enhanced AHP increases the refractory latency of neurons to repolarize and fire again after a burst of APs.
claims.source: Although an enhanced AHP increases the refractory latency of neurons to repolarize and fire again after a burst of APs, the faster repolarization observed for Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons may counterbalance this effect.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on known neurophysiological principles.

claims.claim: The faster repolarization observed for Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons may counterbalance the effect of enhanced AHP.
claims.source: Although an enhanced AHP increases the refractory latency of neurons to repolarize and fire again after a burst of APs, the faster repolarization observed for Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons may counterbalance this effect.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The changes in AP properties account for more APs fired within bursts, whereas enhanced post-burst AHPs dampen spontaneous firing between bursts.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with enhanced phasic burst firing in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons. The changes in AP properties account for more APs fired within bursts, whereas enhanced post-burst AHPs dampen spontaneous firing between bursts (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 2.

claims.claim: Previous studies have shown that blocking M-current in rodent cortical excitatory neurons acutely with XE991 enhances neuronal excitability by lowering AP threshold, impairing AP repolarization and attenuating the post-burst AHP.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that blocking M-current in rodent cortical excitatory neurons acutely with XE991 enhances neuronal excitability by lowering AP threshold, impairing AP repolarization and attenuating the post-burst AHP (Yue and Yaari, 2004; Santini and Porter, 2010; Lezmy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: XE991 significantly lowered AP threshold and slowed AP repolarization in control neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports (Yue and Yaari, 2004; Santini and Porter, 2010; Lezmy et al., 2017), XE991 significantly lowered AP threshold and slowed AP repolarization (AP threshold: p=0.0104; HW: p=0.0046; fAHP: p=0.009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E and citations.

claims.claim: XE991 blunted the mAHP and sAHP amplitudes in control neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, XE991 blunted the mAHP and sAHP amplitudes in these neurons (mAHP: p=0.0014; sAHP: p=0.022; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claims.claim: The effects of acute XE991 treatment did not resemble the behavior of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons, suggesting that loss of M-current alone is not sufficient for phasic burst firing.
claims.source: These effects did not resemble the behavior of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons, suggesting that loss of M-current alone is not sufficient for phasic burst firing.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: KCNQ2-DEE neurons develop a more pronounced phasic bursting phenotype progressively as a result of chronic M-current reduction coupled with dyshomeostatic adaptation of intrinsic membrane properties at different temporal scales.
claims.source: Collectively, these experiments suggest that KCNQ2-DEE neurons develop a more pronounced phasic bursting phenotype progressively as a result of chronic M-current reduction coupled with dyshomeostatic adaptation of intrinsic membrane properties at different temporal scales.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of this section, based on the totality of experimental data.

claims.claim: Strong candidates for dyshomeostatic mechanisms are large, intermediate, and small conductance, Ca2+- and voltage-gated BK (KCNMA1) and IK/SK (KCNN4/KCNN1-3) channels that participate in fast AP repolarization and slow Ca2+-dependent post-burst AHP, respectively.
claims.source: While a number of different channels might contribute to a dyshomeostatic mechanism, strong candidates are large, intermediate, and small conductance, Ca2+- and voltage-gated BK (KCNMA1) and IK/SK (KCNN4/KCNN1-3) channels that participate in fast AP repolarization and slow Ca2+-dependent post-burst AHP, respectively (Storm, 1990; Iyer et al., 2017; Latorre et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: On week 3, KCNMA1 (BK channel), KCNN4 (IK channel), and KCNA4 (encoding KV1.4 channel) expression was higher in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.source: By contrast, KCNMA1 (BK channel), KCNN4 (IK channel), and KCNA4 (encoding KV1.4 channel) expression was higher in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons (p=0.0429, p=0.016 and p=0.0216, respectively; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: By week 5, the difference in KCNMA1, KCNN4 and KCNA4 was no longer significant but other differences had emerged, including an upregulation of KCNMB3, KCNN1, KCNN2, KCNA1, and KCNA2, and downregulation of KCNQ5 expression in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons relative to controls.
claims.source: By week 5, the difference in KCNMA1, KCNN4 and KCNA4 was no longer significant but other differences had emerged, including an upregulation of KCNMB3, KCNN1, KCNN2, KCNA1, and KCNA2, and downregulation of KCNQ5 expression in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons relative to controls (p=0.0081, p<0.0001, p=0.018, p=0.0099, p=0.0017 and p=0.0198, respectively; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: These genes, which encode a BK channel β-subunit, SK channels (SK1 and SK2), KV1.1 and KV1.2, respectively, have been implicated in epilepsy and developmental delay in human and animal studies.
claims.source: These genes, which encode a BK channel β-subunit, SK channels (SK1 and SK2), KV1.1 and KV1.2, respectively, have been implicated in epilepsy and developmental delay in human and animal studies (Hu et al., 2003; Lorenz et al., 2007; McKay et al., 2012; Lerche et al., 2013; Masnada et al., 2017; Paulhus et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The upregulation of KCNMB3, KCNN1, KCNN2, KCNA1, and KCNA2 is consistent with a gain of a K+ conductance suggested by electrophysiological studies.
claims.source: and their upregulation is consistent with a gain of a K+ conductance suggested by our electrophysiological studies (i.e. BK/SK upregulation can lead to larger post-burst AHPs and BK/KV1.1/KV1.2 upregulation can lead to faster AP repolarization).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Addition of apamin reduced the mAHP in both Q2-04R581Q/+ and isoQ2-04+/+ neurons, and reduced the sAHP only in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.source: Addition of apamin (500 nM), a SK channel antagonist, reduced the mAHP in both groups, and reduced the sAHP only in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The magnitudes of change of the mAHP and sAHP were significantly larger for Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons compared to isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: The magnitudes of change of the mAHP (ΔmAHP: p=0.0001) and sAHP (ΔsAHP: p<0.0001) were significantly larger for Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons compared to isoQ2-04+/+ neurons (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claims.claim: Functional enhancement of SK channels in KCNQ2-DEE neurons contributes to the increase of slowly deactivating Ca2+-activated currents that determine the level of post-burst AHP.
claims.source: These data suggest that functional enhancement of SK channels in KCNQ2-DEE neurons contributes to the increase of slowly deactivating Ca2+-activated currents that determine the level of post-burst AHP.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Blocking SK and BK channels reduced the ISI CoV of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons to the level observed in untreated controls.
claims.source: Blocking SK and BK channels reduced the ISI CoV of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons (p=0.0015) to the level observed in untreated controls, while treatment did not affect isoQ2-04+/+ neurons (p=0.796; Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Addition of apamin and paxilline had a significantly larger effect on the number of spikes/burst and burst % in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons than in isogenic control neurons.
claims.source: Addition of both drugs also had a significantly larger effect on the number of spikes/burst (ΔSpikes/Burst: p=0.0087) and burst % (ΔBurst%: p=0.0254) in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons than in isogenic control neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Pharmacological treatment with apamin and paxilline specifically reduced the bursting features to the levels seen in isogenic control neurons before drug application.
claims.source: This pharmacological treatment specifically reduced the bursting features to the levels seen in isogenic control neurons before drug application (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of SK and BK channels in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons reduces post-burst AHPs and normalizes phasic burst firing behavior.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that inhibition of SK and BK channels in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons reduces post-burst AHPs and normalizes phasic burst firing behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Chronically XE991-treated control neurons exhibited enhanced repolarization and larger post-burst AHPs relative to untreated controls.
claims.source: Chronically XE991-treated control neurons exhibited enhanced repolarization (half width: p=0.0002; fAHP: p=0.01) and larger post-burst AHPs (mAHP: p=0.0001; sAHP: p=0.0008) relative to untreated controls (Figure 6B–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B and Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B and Table 2.

claims.claim: The effects of chronic XE991 treatment were identical to or larger than the properties observed for untreated Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.source: Importantly, these effects were identical to or larger than the properties observed for untreated Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Chronic XE991 treatment effectively phenocopied the electrophysiological behavior of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons in isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: This experimental paradigm effectively phenocopied the electrophysiological behavior of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons in isoQ2-04+/+ neurons and suggests that the enhanced AP repolarization and larger post-burst AHP that we identified in KCNQ2-DEE neurons, occur as a result of long-term reduction of M-current.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The enhanced AP repolarization and larger post-burst AHP identified in KCNQ2-DEE neurons occur as a result of long-term reduction of M-current.
claims.source: This experimental paradigm effectively phenocopied the electrophysiological behavior of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons in isoQ2-04+/+ neurons and suggests that the enhanced AP repolarization and larger post-burst AHP that we identified in KCNQ2-DEE neurons, occur as a result of long-term reduction of M-current.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Within 24 hr of adding XE991 to the neuronal media, there was an increase in the number of active electrodes approximately three times higher in XE991-treated relative to untreated isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: Within 24 hr of adding XE991 to the neuronal media (DIV: 12-13), we observed an increase in the number of active electrodes approximately three times higher in XE991-treated relative to untreated isoQ2-04+/+ neurons (p<0.0001; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C.

claims.claim: Within 24 hr of adding XE991, there was a sevenfold increase in burst % in XE991-treated isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: This was accompanied by a sevenfold increase in burst % (p<0.0001; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: The magnitude of change in mean firing frequency on active electrodes was not significantly affected by XE991 in isoQ2-04+/+ neurons.
claims.source: However, the magnitude of change in mean firing frequency on active electrodes was not significantly affected by XE991 in isoQ2-04+/+ neurons (p=0.4557; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: XE991 induced a relatively fast upregulation of spontaneously firing isoQ2-04+/+ neurons to the levels of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons.
claims.source: Thus, XE991 induced a relatively fast upregulation of spontaneously firing isoQ2-04+/+ neurons to the levels of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Chronic M-current inhibition led to long-term enhanced burst firing parameters such as ISI CoV, number of bursting electrodes and bursts, number of spikes per burst and burst %.
claims.source: Furthermore, chronic M-current inhibition led to long-term enhanced burst firing parameters such as ISI CoV, number of bursting electrodes and bursts, number of spikes per burst and burst % (p<0.0001, p=0.0011, p=0.0275, p<0.0001, p<0.0001, respectively; Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The effects of chronic M-current inhibition on bursting in control neurons were more dramatic than the inherent bursting phenotype in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons, likely because of the less severe loss of function associated with the mutation relative to the pharmacological treatment with XE991.
claims.source: The effects of chronic M-current inhibition on bursting in control neurons were more dramatic than the inherent bursting phenotype in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons, likely because of the less severe loss of function associated with the mutation relative to the pharmacological treatment with XE991 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by Figure 1B.

results.result: KCNQ2 mutations cause a spectrum of epileptic disorders including benign familial neonatal seizures (BFNS) and the more severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), with KCNQ2 mutations accounting for approximately 5% of all genetic epilepsy mutations and 10% of early-onset DEE cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C18 establish well-documented background knowledge about KCNQ2-related epilepsies, supported by multiple citations to prior literature. These claims provide essential context for the disease being studied and are consistently reported in the epilepsy literature.

results.result: KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 form heterotetrameric channels that mediate the M-current, which dampens neuronal excitability by activating near action potential threshold and contributing to post-burst afterhyperpolarization. These channels are enriched at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 describe established biophysical properties of KCNQ2/3 channels, supported by multiple citations to foundational studies. This background information is well-established in the ion channel literature and provides necessary context for understanding the experimental findings.

results.result: A patient with KCNQ2-DEE was identified carrying a de novo heterozygous R581Q mutation in a highly conserved coiled-coil domain of KCNQ2, a mutation previously observed in multiple other DEE cases and known to be critical for channel function.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 describe the patient mutation and its location in the protein structure, supported by clinical sequencing data (Figure 1A) and database information (ClinVar). The conservation of the residue and prior reports of similar mutations strengthen the clinical relevance of this variant.

results.result: The R581Q mutation produces a loss-of-function effect, with 81.6% and 56.6% reduction in current density in homozygous and heterozygous configurations, respectively, when expressed in CHO cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by heterologous expression data in Figure 1B showing statistically significant reductions in current density (p<0.0001 and p=0.006). The use of both homozygous and heterozygous configurations appropriately models the patient's genetic state.

results.result: Patient-derived iPSCs were generated and an isogenic control line was created using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, with comprehensive validation showing no off-target effects and normal pluripotency markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 describe rigorous iPSC generation and validation methods. The use of whole genome sequencing (29-28x coverage) and T7 endonuclease assays for all 74 predicted off-target sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) provides strong evidence for the specificity of gene editing. The isogenic control design is a major strength of the study.

results.result: iPSCs were differentiated into cortical excitatory neurons using NGN2 overexpression, with >95% of cells expressing neuronal markers (MAP2, vGLUT1) and characteristic layer 2/3 cortical markers (vGLUT2, FOXG1, BRN2), and expressing KCNQ2 splice variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 describe the neuronal differentiation protocol and characterization, supported by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1F-G) and RT-qPCR data (Figure 1H). The high efficiency (>95%) and expression of appropriate markers validate the neuronal identity, though the model is limited to excitatory neurons.

results.result: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited enhanced spontaneous activity early in maturation (DIV 10-13) and developed progressively more pronounced phasic burst firing over time, with increased number of bursts, spikes per burst, and percentage of spikes occurring in bursts compared to isogenic controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C53 are supported by longitudinal MEA recordings (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.0001 for multiple parameters). The progressive nature of the phenotype is well-documented across multiple time points. However, the study would benefit from additional biological replicates (N=3 differentiations reported).

results.result: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons initially showed properties consistent with M-current loss (depolarized RMP, increased input resistance, slower AP repolarization at week 3), but progressively developed faster AP repolarization and larger fast AHP by weeks 4-5, suggesting compensatory changes beyond simple M-current loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 are supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings at three time points (Figure 3, Table 1) with appropriate statistical comparisons. The temporal evolution from slower to faster AP repolarization is a key finding. However, the interpretation of 'compensatory' mechanisms (C61) is somewhat speculative and requires additional mechanistic validation.

results.result: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons exhibited significantly larger medium and slow post-burst afterhyperpolarizations (mAHP and sAHP) compared to controls at weeks 4-5, which together with faster AP repolarization could account for the phasic burst firing pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by experimental data (Figure 3E-F, Table 1) showing statistically significant differences in AHP measurements (p<0.0001). The interpretation linking these properties to burst firing (C67) is reasonable but somewhat inferential. The time-dependent attenuation of AHP in controls (C64) is an interesting observation that strengthens the case for altered developmental trajectory.

results.result: Acute M-current blockade with XE991 in control neurons produced effects (lowered AP threshold, slowed repolarization, reduced AHP) that differed from the Q2-04R581Q/+ phenotype, suggesting that chronic M-current loss triggers additional adaptive mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by acute XE991 experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-G) showing opposite effects on AP properties compared to patient neurons. This is a critical control experiment that strengthens the interpretation of dyshomeostatic adaptation. However, the acute vs. chronic comparison could be confounded by differences in drug concentration or exposure duration.

results.result: KCNQ2-DEE neurons develop phasic bursting through chronic M-current reduction coupled with dyshomeostatic adaptation involving BK and SK channels that mediate fast AP repolarization and slow Ca2+-dependent post-burst AHP.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 represent the main mechanistic conclusion, supported by the totality of electrophysiological data and prior literature on BK/SK channel function. However, the term 'dyshomeostatic' implies maladaptive compensation, which requires additional evidence to distinguish from potentially protective homeostatic responses.

results.result: Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons showed temporally dynamic changes in K+ channel gene expression, with upregulation of KCNMA1, KCNN4, and KCNA4 at week 3, followed by upregulation of KCNMB3, KCNN1, KCNN2, KCNA1, and KCNA2 at week 5, consistent with enhanced K+ conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing statistically significant differences at specific time points. The temporal dynamics are interesting, though the study would benefit from protein-level validation. The interpretation linking gene expression to functional changes (C77) is reasonable but somewhat inferential without direct measurement of channel protein levels or single-channel properties.

results.result: Apamin (SK channel antagonist) reduced mAHP and sAHP more strongly in Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons than controls, demonstrating functional enhancement of SK channels contributing to increased post-burst AHP.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 5A-C) showing significantly larger effects of apamin in patient neurons (p=0.0001 for ΔmAHP, p<0.0001 for ΔsAHP). This provides direct functional evidence for SK channel upregulation beyond gene expression data. The experimental design appropriately uses magnitude of drug effect rather than absolute values.

results.result: Combined blockade of SK and BK channels with apamin and paxilline normalized the bursting phenotype of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons to control levels, reducing ISI CoV, spikes per burst, and burst percentage.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by MEA recordings with acute drug application (Figure 5D) showing statistically significant rescue effects. This is a critical result demonstrating that BK/SK upregulation is functionally important for the bursting phenotype. However, the rescue is not complete for all parameters, and the interpretation of 'normalization' should be qualified.

results.result: Chronic treatment of control neurons with XE991 (1 µM) phenocopied the electrophysiological properties of Q2-04R581Q/+ neurons, including enhanced AP repolarization and larger post-burst AHPs, demonstrating that these changes result from long-term M-current reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by chronic XE991 experiments (Figure 6B-E, Table 2) showing similar or larger effects than patient neurons. This is a key experiment establishing causality between chronic M-current loss and the observed phenotype. However, the pharmacological model may not perfectly recapitulate the genetic mutation, and the concentration used (1 µM) may produce stronger effects than the partial loss-of-function mutation.

results.result: Chronic XE991 treatment rapidly increased the number of active neurons and burst firing within 24 hours, and led to long-term enhancement of burst firing parameters that were more dramatic than the inherent Q2-04R581Q/+ phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 are supported by MEA data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6F) showing rapid and sustained effects of chronic XE991. The observation that pharmacological blockade produces stronger effects than the mutation (C94) is appropriately interpreted as reflecting the partial loss-of-function nature of R581Q. The temporal dynamics (24 hr vs. weeks) provide insight into the time course of adaptation.

results.result: Chronic XE991 treatment upregulated expression of KCNMA1, KCNMB3, KCNN1, KCNN2, KCNN4, KCNA1, and HCN1 at week 5, and acute BK/SK blockade rescued the bursting phenotype in both Q2-04R581Q/+ and chronically XE991-treated neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 6G) and pharmacological rescue experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The parallel findings in genetic and pharmacological models strengthen the conclusion that BK/SK upregulation is a consequence of reduced M-current. However, the study would benefit from examining whether preventing BK/SK upregulation blocks the development of the bursting phenotype.

results.result: Neurons with KCNQ2 loss-of-function mutations exhibit progressive escalation of burst firing and develop intrinsic membrane properties (faster AP repolarization, enhanced AHP) not previously associated with M-current loss, suggesting dyshomeostatic plasticity alters neurodevelopmental trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive electrophysiological, molecular, and pharmacological data. The progressive nature of the phenotype and the identification of compensatory mechanisms are well-supported. However, the term 'dyshomeostatic' implies maladaptive changes, which requires additional evidence to distinguish from potentially protective responses. The study would also benefit from examining whether these changes occur in vivo.

results.result: Patient iPSC-derived neurons exhibit faster action potential repolarization, larger post-burst afterhyperpolarization, and functional enhancement of Ca2+-activated K+ channels, which can be recapitulated by chronic M-current inhibition and facilitate a burst-suppression firing pattern reminiscent of patient EEG patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C7 summarize the main findings stated in the abstract, which are supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2-6). The burst-suppression pattern is well-documented by MEA recordings, and the link to patient EEG patterns (C6) is supported by citations, though direct comparison with patient EEG data would strengthen this claim.

results.result: KCNQ2-DEE neurons exhibit burst firing patterns reminiscent of interictal EEG patterns in patients, characterized by increased spikes per burst and longer refractory periods between bursts, representing an alteration in discharge pattern rather than simply increased neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 interpret the experimental findings in the context of clinical epilepsy, supported by MEA data and citations to EEG studies. The distinction between altered firing pattern vs. increased activity (C106) is an important conceptual point supported by the data. However, the comparison to patient EEG (C105) is somewhat inferential, as direct recordings from patient neurons are not available.

results.result: Homeostatic plasticity in response to chronic hyperexcitability or M-current loss has been observed in multiple systems, including mouse models and cultured neurons, and may be cell-type specific, with evidence that similar adaptive changes occur in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C114 provide context from prior literature on homeostatic plasticity, supported by multiple citations. These claims appropriately situate the current findings within the broader field. The discussion of cell-type specificity (C113) and in vivo relevance (C110) is important for interpreting the iPSC model results.

results.result: Homeostatic plasticity can become maladaptive and pathogenic, and the findings are concordant with previous work on homeostatic responses to chronic M-current inhibition, with examples of acquired channelopathies developing during epilepsy.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 discuss the concept of maladaptive homeostasis and acquired channelopathies, supported by citations to prior literature. These claims provide important conceptual framework for interpreting the results. However, distinguishing between adaptive and maladaptive responses requires additional functional evidence beyond the current study.

results.result: Suppression of M-current leads to rearrangement of neuronal properties on different temporal scales, with rapid effects on burst firing (24 hr) but slower changes in AP repolarization (weeks), emphasizing the importance of examining firing patterns rather than just firing frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 synthesize the temporal dynamics observed in the study, supported by the chronic XE991 experiments. The emphasis on firing pattern vs. frequency (C122) is an important conceptual contribution. The interpretation of multiple temporal scales (C123) is well-supported by the data, though the molecular mechanisms underlying these different time courses remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: KCNQ2-DEE neurons initially exhibit properties consistent with M-current loss but progressively develop faster AP repolarization associated with upregulation of KCNMB3, KCNA1, and KCNA2, suggesting maladaptive upregulation of fast voltage-gated K+ conductances.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C129 integrate the temporal evolution of electrophysiological properties with gene expression changes. The interpretation linking KCNMB3 upregulation to faster AP repolarization (C127) is supported by prior literature on β3 subunit function. However, the study would benefit from direct measurement of BK channel inactivation kinetics and protein-level validation of the gene expression changes.

results.result: The enhanced post-burst AHP in KCNQ2-DEE neurons is mediated by Ca2+-activated K+ channels, with evidence for upregulation of SK channels (KCNN1, KCNN2) and multiple developmentally regulated mechanisms involving BK and IK channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C138 discuss the mechanisms underlying enhanced AHP, supported by gene expression data, pharmacological experiments, and prior literature on Ca2+-activated K+ channels. The interpretation of multiple mechanisms (C136) is reasonable given the temporal dynamics of different channel expression. However, direct measurement of intracellular Ca2+ dynamics would strengthen the interpretation of activity-dependent contributions (C135).

results.result: Both SK and BK channels contribute to increased K+ conductance in KCNQ2-DEE neurons, and while increased K+ conductance is not traditionally associated with epilepsy, gain-of-function mutations in multiple K+ channels have been reported in genetic epilepsy.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 discuss the paradoxical role of K+ channel upregulation in epilepsy, supported by pharmacological data and citations to prior literature. This is an important conceptual point that challenges traditional views of epilepsy mechanisms. The citations to gain-of-function K+ channel mutations in epilepsy (C142) provide important context.

results.result: Targeting dyshomeostatically altered ion currents might offer an alternative therapeutic strategy for KCNQ2-DEE, particularly if treatment is started late in disease course, and the iPSC platform may be valuable for identifying therapeutics.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 discuss therapeutic implications, which are speculative and not directly tested in the study. While the pharmacological rescue experiments (C81-C84) provide proof-of-concept, the clinical relevance of targeting BK/SK channels in patients is uncertain. The suggestion that late treatment might not be effective (C143) is reasonable but not directly supported by the data. These claims represent future directions rather than established results.

results.result: The earliest hypothesis for KCNQ2 epilepsy posited that loss of channel function leads to increased repetitive firing, but some variants produce gain-of-function effects that could hyperpolarize the AIS and increase AP activation and repolarization rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 provide background on prior hypotheses about KCNQ2 epilepsy mechanisms, supported by citations. These claims appropriately contextualize the current findings within the evolution of understanding in the field. The discussion of gain-of-function variants (C20) is important for understanding the complexity of KCNQ2-related disorders.

results.result: One clinical hallmark of KCNQ2-DEE is an interictal burst-suppression pattern recorded by EEG during the first few days of life.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 describes a well-established clinical feature of KCNQ2-DEE, supported by citations to clinical studies. This provides important clinical context for interpreting the burst firing patterns observed in the iPSC-derived neurons.
